title: Chemical Kinetics: The Study of Reaction Rates

questions.question: For the reaction 2N2O5 -> 4NO2 + O2, the rate of disappearance of N2O5 is 0.02 mol per litre per second. The rate of formation of NO2 is:
questions.rationale: Rate = -(1/2)d[N2O5]/dt = +(1/4)d[NO2]/dt. So d[NO2]/dt = 2 x 0.02 = 0.04 mol per litre per second — the stoichiometric factor converts one rate into the other.

questions.question: The units of the rate constant of a first-order reaction are:
questions.rationale: For first order, rate = k[A], so k = rate/[A] has units (mol L-1 s-1)/(mol L-1) = s-1. Zero order gives mol L-1 s-1, second order gives L mol-1 s-1.

questions.question: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 10 minutes. The time required for 75 percent completion is:
questions.rationale: 75 percent completion leaves 25 percent, which is two half-lives worth of decay: 10 + 10 = 20 minutes. Each half-life halves the remainder, so after n half-lives, (1/2)^n of the reactant survives.

questions.question: The order of a reaction:
options: Is always equal to the sum of stoichiometric coefficients
Is determined experimentally and can be zero or fractional
Is always equal to the molecularity
questions.rationale: Order comes from experiment, not from the balanced equation, and can be zero or fractional (as in the H2 + Br2 chain reaction). Molecularity, by contrast, applies to elementary steps and is always 1, 2, or 3.

questions.question: For a zero-order reaction, the rate constant k equals:
options: The rate itself, independent of concentration
The slope of the rate-versus-1/T plot
questions.rationale: Zero order: rate = k[A]^0 = k. The rate is constant regardless of concentration, and the concentration falls linearly with time. Photochemical reactions on saturated surfaces show this behaviour.

questions.question: A rise of 10 K roughly doubles the rate of a reaction. The main reason is:
options: Collision frequency barely changes; the fraction of molecules exceeding the activation energy grows sharply
The activation energy decreases with temperature
questions.rationale: A 10 K rise changes collision frequency only a few percent. The dramatic effect comes from the Maxwell-Boltzmann tail: exponentially more molecules cross the activation-energy barrier (Arrhenius, k = A e^(-Ea/RT)).

questions.question: Which statement about a catalyst is FALSE?
options: It speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally
It shifts the equilibrium position toward more products
It is regenerated chemically unchanged at the end
questions.rationale: A catalyst provides a faster pathway with lower Ea for BOTH directions, so equilibrium is reached sooner but its position (the equilibrium constant) is untouched. It never makes an unfavourable reaction favourable.

questions.question: In the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(-Ea/RT), a plot of log k versus 1/T is a straight line whose slope equals:
questions.rationale: log k = log A - (Ea/2.303R)(1/T). Comparing with y = c + mx, the slope is -Ea/2.303R. Measuring slopes at several temperatures is the standard way to determine activation energy.

questions.question: The rate law for a reaction is rate = k[A]^1/2[B]^3/2. The overall order of the reaction is:
questions.rationale: Overall order = sum of exponents = 1/2 + 3/2 = 2. Individual orders may be fractional, and their sum gives the overall order — here exactly two.

questions.question: A first-order reaction is 20 percent complete in 10 minutes. The half-life of the reaction is approximately:
questions.rationale: k = (2.303/t) log(100/80) = (2.303/10)(0.0969) about 0.0223 per minute. Then t-half = 0.693/k about 31 minutes. Since each half-life reduces the remainder by half, 20 percent gone is well under one half-life of decay.
